pages.heading: A letter from the editor
body: Lisbon does not announce itself. It reveals itself slowly: a tiled facade catching the afternoon sun, a tram bell somewhere below, the smell of grilled sardines drifting up a staircase that seems to lead nowhere in particular.

We came for a long weekend and kept finding reasons to stay. This guide is the route we wish someone had handed us at the airport: unhurried, a little steep, and full of places where the person behind the counter remembers your order by the second visit.
Wear good shoes. Say obrigado. Get lost on purpose.
pages.quote: Get lost on purpose. The best table in Lisbon is the one you weren't looking for.

pages.heading: Lisbon at a glance
tips: Buy a rechargeable Viva Viagem card at any metro station.
Shops close early on Sundays; plan lunch accordingly.
The light is best an hour before sunset. Climb something.

pages.heading: The lay of the land
legend: Baixa: the grid below the hills
Bairro Alto: nightlife on steep streets
LX Factory: creative reuse by the river

pages.heading: Alfama
pages.story: The oldest district survived the 1755 earthquake and shows it: a maze of whitewashed lanes, laundry strung between balconies, and fado spilling from doorways after dark. Come early, before the tour groups, and walk downhill.
places: Terracotta rooftops to the river. Bring a coffee.
Romanesque cathedral, free to enter the nave.

pages.heading: Chiado & Bairro Alto
pages.story: Poets, bookshops and the grand cafés of Chiado give way, after sunset, to the beautifully chaotic street party of Bairro Alto. Same hill, two personalities.
places: The world's oldest operating bookshop, since 1732.
Order a bica under the bronze poet.
A Gothic nave open to the sky.
Quiet garden terrace, great at dusk.

pages.heading: Belém
pages.story: Lisbon's age of discovery in stone: monasteries, towers and a monument to the navigators, all along a breezy riverside promenade. Go on a weekday morning.
places: Manueline masterpiece; book the cloister ticket online.
The original custard tart, warm, with cinnamon.
Climb for river views; queues build after 11.
Lift to the top for the whole bay.

pages.heading: Eat & Drink
items: Chef stalls under one roof. Good for indecision.
Tiger prawns, then a steak sandwich to finish.
Watch the tarts come out of the oven.
A shot of cherry liqueur, standing.
Small plates, daily blackboard, no bookings.
pages.note: Hours and prices change often. Verify before you go.

pages.heading: Ride the 28
pages.body: Tram 28 rattles through Graça, Alfama, Baixa and Estrela on a route older than most countries' railways. Board at Martim Moniz at 8am to get a seat and an empty street.
pages.caption: Yellow trams, steep gradients, zero hurry.

pages.heading: Hidden gems
gems: Locals walk dogs under the palms. No one else is awake.
A bookshop inside a former printing works, complete with a flying bicycle.
The highest viewpoint in the city and the least crowded.
A former brothel turned cocktail bar. Velvet and mischief.

pages.heading: Three days, unhurried
days: Walk up to Alfama via the Sé

pages.heading: Good to know
sections: Metro is fast and cheap; trams are for fun.
Uber and Bolt are inexpensive after dark.
Wear flat shoes: the cobbles are slippery.
Coperto (table snacks) is charged only if eaten.
Greet shopkeepers: bom dia, boa tarde.
Keep voices low on trams and in churches.
